newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - UAL poised for strong Q1, year.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - UAL poised for strong Q1, year.

text.p: United Airlines, with a quick resolution to its labor problems, is poised to post strong profits and traffic growth in 1997, analysts said.

The tentative labor accord reached late Monday with its pilots and machinists eases the recent uncertainty hovering over United. The pact will free the airline to focus on its bottom line, industry experts said.

"The difficulties between the company and labor are in the past, they look forward to building the company again," said Joseph Blasi, a professor at Rutgers University's School of Management and Labor Relations.
Hours after reaching a sooner-than-expected tentative wage agreement, UAL Corp said it expected its first quarter earnings will top Wall Street estimates.
UAL, the parent of United Airlines, said it expects its first quarter earnings to exceed $1.30 per fully distributed share. A year earlier the airline earned $0.77 a share.
United's bullish forecast set an upbeat tone for the rest of the sector, boosting stock prices on Tuesday.
UAL gained 4 to 63-7/8, Delta Air Lines Inc added 1 to 83-14 and Continental Airlines Inc increased 5/8 to 29-5/8. The Dow Jones transport index added more than 31 points to 2404.
UAL also said its February load factor rose to 68.4 percent from 66.3 percent.
Domestic airlines have benefitted from the lapse of the passenger excise tax and labor disruption at AMR Corp's American Airlines, analysts said.
Throughout the industry, first quarter revenues and load factors will likely be stronger than year-ago results. On Tuesday, several carriers posted February load factor gains.
American Airline's labor strife created a first quarter windfall for rival carriers, especially United, analysts said. Passengers shied away from American as the February 15 strike deadline loomed.

"Some airlines benefitted from the disruptions at American. United and American share a hub in Chicago, so United got a boost for about a week to 10 days," said Jeffrey Long, an analyst with J.P. Morgan.
United attributed only part of its expected first quarter success to American's pilots strike.

"While the threat of a strike at a major competitor was of some benefit to United, the more important message is that our traffic grew nearly four percent in a strong domestic pricing environment," said John Edwardson, United's president and chief operating officer.
Edward Starkman, an airline analyst with Dillon Read, said United made the most of strong consumer demand and a stable pricing environment.
"It's the nature of their strong route and hub structure. They can make the most of an upswing," Starkman said.
United has been particularly adept at targeting its discounts to specific routes and times and controlling its growth.

United and other airlines have also culled extra revenues since January 1 by pocketing the 10 percent tax that would normally go the federal government. The tax is expected to be reinstated within the next few days.

The tax was absent last year as well. Airlines initially passed on the savings to consumers, but then slowly raised fares throughout the year. This year, airlines are keeping the extra money for themselves.
Carriers may try to raise fares when the tax is reinstated. If consumers balk, carriers may have to increase fares more slowly, analysts said.
